analysis.one_liner: Strengthens penalties and enforcement for employers who pay women less than men for equal work.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Education and the Workforce Committee and its subcommittees for the rest of the two-year Congress, despite 122 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Equal Pay Act's enforcement rules. Employers who pay a woman less than a man for equal work would face compensatory and punitive damages, not just back pay, and workers could sue as a class. It would make it illegal to fire or punish an employee for asking about or sharing wage information, add training and research programs, and create a voluntary award for employers who fix pay gaps.
analysis.who_benefits: Women who are paid less than men for work requiring equal skill, effort, and responsibility would gain a real remedy: damages beyond back pay, class actions, protection against being fired for discussing wages, and better-trained enforcement agencies.

how_it_helps.text: Adds compensatory and punitive damages for Equal Pay Act violations, so a worker who wins is not merely restored to where she started but actually compensated [S3].
Protects employees who ask about or disclose wages from retaliation, which is the practical precondition for ever discovering a pay gap [S3].
Allows Equal Pay Act claims to be maintained as class actions and lets the Labor Secretary seek damages on workers' behalf, making enforcement feasible against large employers [S3].

Requires the EEOC and the federal contract compliance office to train staff and affected parties on wage discrimination, and directs the Labor Secretary to study and publicize ways to close pay disparities [S2].
Creates voluntary job-evaluation guidelines and a national award recognizing employers who raise women's pay fairly rather than lowering men's [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay women less than men for equal work would bear new liability, larger damages, class-action exposure, and possible technical-assistance and reporting costs.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' with no cost estimate, so the expense of new Labor Department programs, training, and studies is left open [S3].

Expanded punitive damages and class-action availability would raise litigation exposure for employers broadly, including ones with no intent to discriminate, since Equal Pay Act claims do not require proof of intent.
The nonretaliation and disclosure provisions let employees share individual wage data, which some employers view as a privacy and confidentiality concern for co-workers as well as the company.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers facing pay discrimination, the added damages, class actions, and wage-discussion protections materially change an enforcement system that until now mostly returned only unpaid wages. The costs fall mainly on employers who underpay women; the main honest objection is that broader litigation exposure could reach employers with unintentional gaps, and the bill leaves its own administrative costs uncapped.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to two of its subcommittees, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on February 3, 1999, joined by House Democratic leader Richard Gephardt and 23 other original cosponsors [S1] [S3].
It accumulated 122 cosponsors: 120 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 1 Republican [S4].

The only actions ever taken were a referral to the Education and the Workforce Committee on the day of introduction and, a month later, referrals to the Employer-Employee Relations and Workforce Protections subcommittees [S5].
No hearing, committee vote, or House floor action is recorded for the bill through the end of the 106th Congress in January 2001 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay women less than men for equal work were better off, because the stronger penalties, class actions, and wage-discussion protections never took effect. No worker gained anything from the bill's death.

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Paycheck Fairness Act and gathered 24 original cosponsors including the House Democratic leader.

for.name: 1 House Republican and 1 Independent
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a small minority-party footprint.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to two subcommittees and never scheduled a hearing or markup on it.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic: 120 of the 122 cosponsors were Democrats, with just one Republican and one Independent signing on, and the Republican-controlled committee and floor process never advanced it.

industries.note: The bill would expose them to compensatory and punitive damages, class actions, and liability whenever employees discuss wages. Its benefits to women workers come directly out of those employers' pay practices, so its interest runs against the workers it protects.

Even employers without pay gaps would face broader litigation exposure under expanded class actions and damages, and small new compliance burdens from training and reporting. Employers who close gaps voluntarily could earn a federal award.
